title: The Default Threshold

scenario.situation: The churn model ships with a 0.5 decision threshold. Retention spend feels wasted — too many customers offered discounts end up staying anyway, and churners still slip through.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The team concludes the model isn't accurate enough and wants to retrain on more data or try a more complex architecture.
scenario.question: Is low model accuracy really the problem, or is something else driving the poor business outcomes?

decisions.prompt: The team wants a better model. How do you frame the investigation before touching any training data?

options.label: Benchmark the model with additional accuracy metrics
options.detail: Run precision, recall, and F1 at 0.5 to confirm whether the model is truly underperforming.
options.consequence: The model scores reasonably well on F1 at 0.5. This looks like vindication, but you haven't asked whether 0.5 is the right operating point for this business — so the real problem stays hidden.
options.divergenceCost: Accepted the 0.5 default as given and evaluated performance around the wrong operating point.

options.label: Audit the cost structure before touching the model
options.detail: Map the business cost of a missed churner versus a false alarm, then ask whether the threshold was ever set to reflect those costs.
options.consequence: You discover the threshold was never calibrated to cost — it was left at 0.5 by default. This opens the real thread: the model's outputs may be fine, but the decision rule is misaligned with the economics.

options.label: Collect more labeled training data
options.detail: Assume the issue is data volume and scope a labeling effort to retrain.
options.consequence: Weeks of labeling work produce a marginally better model — but retention spend is still wasted because the threshold is still 0.5. The root cause was never touched.
options.divergenceCost: Jumped to a solution before diagnosing the actual failure mode.

options.label: Switch to a more complex model architecture
options.detail: Replace the current model with a gradient-boosted ensemble or a neural net.
options.consequence: A new model is trained and deployed. AUC nudges up slightly, but false-alarm rates and missed churners barely change in production — because the decision rule is still 0.5.
options.divergenceCost: Applied complexity to a calibration problem, not a modeling problem.

decisions.prompt: You've learned a missed churner costs ~$200 in lost revenue while a false alarm costs ~$20 in wasted retention spend. Which view of model performance do you trust to find the right threshold?

artifact.title: Model performance at threshold = 0.5
artifact.caption: Standard classification metrics at the 0.5 default. Accuracy and precision look acceptable — but recall is 61%, meaning 39% of churners are missed entirely.

options.label: Standard classification metrics at 0.5 (accuracy, precision, F1)
options.detail: Use the model's existing evaluation report to judge whether performance is sufficient.
options.consequence: Accuracy is 84% and F1 is 69% — the team argues the model looks fine, which confirms their bias. But these metrics treat every error equally and say nothing about what threshold minimizes business cost.
options.divergenceCost: Used cost-blind metrics to answer a cost-sensitive question.

options.label: Expected cost curve across thresholds (cost-weighted)
options.detail: Compute total expected business cost (missed churners × $200 + false alarms × $20) at every threshold from 0.1 to 0.9 and find the minimum.
options.consequence: The cost curve bottoms out near 0.2, not 0.5. At 0.5 the model misses too many high-cost churners; at 0.2 false alarms rise modestly but the expensive misses collapse. The model is fine — the operating point was wrong.

artifact.title: Expected business cost by decision threshold
artifact.caption: Cost-weighted total (missed churners × $200 + false alarms × $20) per 1,000 predictions. Minimum sits at 0.2 — the 0.5 default nearly doubles the avoidable cost.

decisions.prompt: The cost curve shows 0.2 is the cheaper operating point by a wide margin. What do you tell the team?

options.label: "The model is fine — just lower the threshold to 0.2 and redeploy tonight."
options.detail: Make the prescriptive call and move straight to deployment.
options.consequence: The team lowers the threshold and flags far more customers for outreach. But the cost estimates were rough, and the retention team's capacity wasn't checked — the surge of interventions overwhelms the team and the actual cost ratio shifts. The fix was right in direction but skipped validation.
options.divergenceCost: Acted on estimated costs without validating assumptions or running a controlled test first.

options.label: "The model's discrimination is sound; the 0.5 threshold was never calibrated to our cost structure. A threshold near 0.2 looks optimal given current cost estimates — let's validate those estimates and run a shadow deployment before a full rollout."
options.detail: Surface the finding, flag the cost-estimate uncertainty, and propose a controlled validation step.
options.consequence: The team audits the cost estimates with the finance team (the true ratio holds up) and runs a two-week shadow deployment at 0.2 alongside the live 0.5 model. The shadow path catches 34% more churners at only 12% more retention spend. The redeployment is now evidence-backed.

insight: The model was never broken — it was operating at the wrong point on its own output curve. Because a missed churner costs roughly 10× a false alarm, the cost-minimizing threshold is near 0.2, not the default 0.5. The lesson is that a decision threshold is a business parameter, not a statistical default: it belongs in the cost matrix, not the model config file. Strong analysts audit the decision rule before they question the model.
